t: Exclusive Time of Functions — Stack Simulation Editorial
o: We simulate a single-threaded CPU: logs arrive in chronological order, and at any moment the function on top of the call stack is the one running. A function's *exclusive* time excludes time spent inside nested calls. In Example 1, function 0 runs during timestamps 0–1 (2 units), is suspended while 1 runs 2–5 (4 units), then resumes for timestamp 6 (1 unit), giving [3,4]. Example 2 shows recursion: each of the four segments of execution belongs to function 0, summing to 8. Example 3 mixes recursion and sibling calls. Since logs are already sorted by time and well-formed (every start has a matching end), a single linear pass with a stack suffices — no sorting or searching needed.
k: A 'start' at time t means the previous top-of-stack function ran from its resume/start time up to t; an 'end' at time t means the current function ran through t inclusive.
Use end - start + 1 for an end event and t - prevTime for suspending on a start event — the +1 asymmetry comes from start meaning 'beginning of' and end meaning 'end of' a timestamp.
Keep a running 'prevTime' = the last observed event timestamp so each interval is charged exactly once to exactly one function.

a.i: Simulate every individual timestamp: maintain the stack, and for each unit of time between consecutive log events, add 1 to the exclusive time of the stack top. This directly mirrors the CPU ticking one unit at a time.
s: Parse all logs into (id, type, time) tuples.
Walk a virtual clock from one log's timestamp to the next; at each tick, increment result[stack.top()].
On a start log, push the id after ticking up to that time; on an end log, tick through that time then pop.
a.t: O(L) where L is the number of logs — we process each pair of consecutive events once; parsing adds O(L) string work.
a.sp: O(L) for the parsed events plus O(depth) for the stack.

a.i: Instead of pairing consecutive events, track prevTime = the timestamp of the previous log. On a start, the function currently on top ran from prevTime to t-1, so credit it t - prevTime, then push. On an end, the popping function ran through t inclusive, so credit it t - prevTime + 1, then set prevTime = t + 1. Each unit of CPU time is attributed exactly once.
s: Initialize result array of size n, empty stack, prevTime = 0.
For each log, split into id, type, time.
If type is start: if the stack is non-empty, add time - prevTime to result[top]; push id; set prevTime = time.
If type is end: pop id and add time - prevTime + 1 to result[id]; set prevTime = time + 1.
a.t: O(L) — one pass over the L logs with O(1) work per log (L can be up to ~2n given matching starts/ends).
a.sp: O(d) where d is the maximum call-stack depth (at most L), plus O(n) output.

w: In an interview, go straight to Approach 2 — it is the expected solution and easy to explain: a stack tracks who is running, and prevTime slices CPU time into intervals attributed to whoever was on top. Approach 1 is a fine stepping stone if you struggle with the off-by-one logic. Common pitfalls: forgetting the +1 on end events (start = beginning of timestamp, end = end of timestamp); forgetting to reset prevTime correctly (to t on start, t+1 on end); using the popped id vs. crediting the parent after an end; and integer overflow concerns are minimal here since totals fit in int for these constraints, but use long if timestamps were larger. Edge cases: same function starting immediately after another ends at the same timestamp, recursive calls of the same id, and a call spanning zero visible gap (start followed directly by end at the same timestamp gives 1 unit). Follow-ups might ask about handling out-of-order or malformed logs, or computing total (inclusive) time instead of exclusive time.
